blocks.raw: <ExamTip>The LEA frequently presents Step 2 → Step 3 problems: "Given a slab of these dimensions and this mix design, how many bags of cement are required?" Practice these with a consistent unit discipline. Errors almost always come from unit conversion mistakes — confusing cubic meters with cubic feet, or forgetting to account for waste factors.</ExamTip>

blocks.raw: <Tip>When studying structural systems, always ask: "What does the material need to perform well in this system?" And when studying materials, ask: "What structural system is this material best suited for?" The cross-referencing accelerates both subjects simultaneously.</Tip>

blocks.raw: <Note>The MEPF coordination dimension of LEA-MATL often appears in scenario questions: "The architect is detailing the penetration of a 150mm sanitary drain through a 2-hour rated concrete floor assembly. Which of the following firestopping materials and methods would maintain the floor's fire rating?" These questions reward candidates who studied materials and utilities in conversation with each other.</Note>

blocks.raw: <Tip>Frame the sustainable materials subtopic as a filter you apply to every other materials decision, not a separate topic. Ask: "What is the embodied carbon of this material? Can recycled or regional alternatives achieve the same performance? What are the indoor air quality implications of this finish?" This reframing turns one subtopic into a lens that sharpens all the others.</Tip>

blocks.raw: <Warn>When you encounter a question that seems purely computational, check whether it has a material property condition embedded in it. The "trick" in many LEA estimating questions is that you must first identify the correct material specification (e.g., which cement type, which concrete mix) before you can compute the quantity. Rushing to the arithmetic without reading the scenario carefully is a reliable way to choose the wrong answer.</Warn>
